issues.legal_issue: A joint will disposing of the testators’ properties does not, without language effecting a present transfer, convert their separate or co-owned interests into a joint tenancy; it operates separately on each testator’s death.
material_facts: Three testators executed one document disposing of properties they had acquired separately and jointly, as well as properties they might acquire in the future.
The document allowed the testators to retain possession, control and use of the properties until death and permitted transfers or alienations jointly or separately during their lifetimes.
The beneficiaries were persons other than the testators, and the dispute concerned whether the surviving testator acquired a deceased testator’s properties by survivorship.
The properties held in common by the testators were held as tenants-in-common, not joint tenants.
issues.conclusion: The document was a testamentary disposition, in effect three wills combined in one. Each testator’s properties passed to the named legatees on that testator’s death; the surviving testator did not acquire them by survivorship, and his transfers of the deceased testator’s properties conferred no title.
issues.legal_principle: A joint will is a single document executed by multiple testators but is not thereby a single disposition operating inter vivos or creating joint ownership. It operates on the death of each testator as that testator’s will disposing of that testator’s property. The Court relied on the statements in Halsbury’s Laws of England, 3rd ed., vol. 34, p. 17, para. 12, and Jarman on Wills, 8th ed., p. 41, and on Duddell, In re, Roundway v. Roundway, [1932] 1 Ch. 585, 592. The document’s provision for lifetime control and alienation, including by an individual testator, was inconsistent with a present transfer creating joint ownership. Co-owned properties were held as tenants-in-common, so each testator’s share devolved as that testator’s separate property.

rule.if: civil_title_dispute_under_joint_will and joint_document_disposes_of_multiple_testators_properties and testators_retained_control_until_death and individual_alienation_was_permitted

predicates.civil_title_dispute_under_joint_will: A civil dispute concerns title to property said to pass under a document executed by multiple testators.
predicates.joint_document_disposes_of_multiple_test: One document made by multiple testators purports to dispose of properties belonging to them.
predicates.testators_retained_control_until_death: The document leaves the testators in possession and control of the properties during their lifetimes.
predicates.individual_alienation_was_permitted: The document permits a testator to transfer or alienate property individually during that testator’s lifetime.

issues.definition: When a civil title dispute concerns a joint testamentary document whose makers retain lifetime control and may alienate property individually, each maker’s property passes to the legatee on that maker’s death.

issues.legal_issue: Subsequent conduct of the parties cannot be used to limit or control the meaning of a will whose language is clear and unambiguous.
material_facts: The parties relied on later dealings with the properties and proceedings involving members of the family to argue that they had understood the will to create joint ownership.
Other documents and dealings were also relied on as showing a different understanding of the will.
The Court found the language of the will clear and unambiguous.
issues.conclusion: The evidence of subsequent conduct was inadmissible for the purpose of limiting or controlling the meaning of the will and had to be disregarded.
issues.legal_principle: Where the language of a document is clear and unambiguous, evidence of subsequent conduct cannot be admitted to limit or control its meaning. The Court did not rely on an earlier case for this proposition in the supplied judgment.

predicates.will_construction_dispute: The parties dispute the meaning or effect of a will.
predicates.will_language_is_clear: The court finds that the language of the will is clear and unambiguous.
predicates.later_party_conduct_is_offered_to_contro: A party relies on conduct or dealings after the will was made to limit or control its meaning.

issues.definition: In a dispute over a will, if its language is clear and a party offers later conduct to control its meaning, that conduct is disregarded in construing the will.

issues.legal_issue: A joint will is not a mutual will where the testators do not confer reciprocal benefits on each other and the beneficiaries are distinct from the testators.
material_facts: The document was executed by multiple testators but named other persons as beneficiaries.
The testators did not bequeath property to each other or otherwise confer reciprocal benefits on each other.
The respondents argued that the document could be construed as a mutual will.
issues.conclusion: The document was not a mutual will because its beneficiaries were distinct from its testators and it contained no reciprocal bequests between the testators.
issues.legal_principle: A mutual will exists where two testators confer reciprocal benefits on each other, such as by each making the other a legatee. Where the beneficiaries are distinct from the testators, and there is no reciprocal bequest, the will is not mutual. The Court relied on no earlier case for this proposition in the supplied judgment.

predicates.will_construction_dispute: The parties dispute the meaning or effect of a will.
predicates.beneficiaries_are_distinct_from_testator: The persons who receive benefits under the document are not the persons who executed it as testators.
predicates.no_reciprocal_benefits_are_conferred: The testators do not confer benefits on each other in return for reciprocal benefits.

issues.definition: In a will-construction dispute, a document is not a mutual will when its beneficiaries are distinct from its testators and the testators confer no reciprocal benefits on each other.
